german_b2_apologizing_cultural_misunders.cultural_notes_en:
Cross-cultural apologies follow subtle rules of their own. (1) THE WORD 'SORRY' MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS: in English, 'sorry' can be very light — an attention-getter ('Sorry, can I ask…') with no real admission of fault. In German, 'Entschuldigung' is just as light, but 'Es tut mir leid' is a genuine admission of fault. DO NOT over-use 'Es tut mir leid' when it isn't really your mistake — it reads as weak rather than gracious. (2) APOLOGY = ACCOUNTABILITY: in Germany an apology is expected to carry (a) a concrete acknowledgement of the specific fault, (b) an explanation of the root cause and (c) a plan so it doesn't happen again. NO vague apology. (3) NO LOSS OF FACE: Germans do NOT read an apology as weakness — quite the opposite, an adult is the kind of person who apologises. The British 'stiff upper lip' instinct to brush past mistakes doesn't apply here. A well-formed apology in Germany reads as strength. (4) TIMING: apologise AS SOON AS POSSIBLE after you realise the mistake. Within 24–48 hours is standard. Letting it sit for a week makes the mistake more expensive, not less. (5) IN PERSON > EMAIL: for a serious offence (something personal), apologise face-to-face. Email is only appropriate for minor matters.

Where this diverges from common practice elsewhere: apologies in Vietnam (and often in Anglo-American small-talk) tend to be softer and vaguer ('My bad', 'I wasn't thinking'). German apologies are structured and specific. People who default to the softer style can come across as 'not really sorry'.

In German subsidiaries in Vietnam, workplace conflict resolution usually runs in two stages: (1) immediate de-escalation on the day it happens, then (2) a structured apology + follow-up plan a day or two later. Don't skip stage 2.

One crucial detail: when the mistake is CULTURAL, the framing should be 'kulturelles Missverständnis' — not a personal attack. That frame protects both sides.
german_b2_apologizing_cultural_misunders.tip_advice_en:
The German 5-step apology structure: (1) ACKNOWLEDGE specifically: 'Ich habe X gesagt/getan'. NO vague. (2) RECOGNISE IMPACT: 'Das hat dich Y empfinden lassen'. Show empathy. (3) EXPLAIN context (don't excuse): 'Aus meiner kulturellen Perspektive war es Z gemeint'. (4) APOLOGISE: 'Es tut mir aufrichtig leid'. Once is enough. (5) FORWARD-LOOKING: 'Wie kann ich es wiedergutmachen?'.

Standard phrasing:
- 'Es tut mir aufrichtig leid' — sincere
- 'Das war nicht meine Absicht' — clarify intent
- 'Hätte ich gewusst, hätte ich anders gehandelt' — accountability
- 'Asche auf mein Haupt' (idiom) — formal admission
- 'Reinen Wein einschenken' (idiom) — signalling transparency

Avoid:
- 'Sorry, ich bin nur Vietnamesin' — reads as weak
- 'Aber bei uns ist das normal' — defensive
- 'Es war doch nicht so schlimm' — minimising
- 'Du hast es auch missverstanden' — counter-attack
- Five 'sorrys' in a row — Germans read this as insincere

When the other side apologises to YOU: (1) Accept gracefully: 'Vielen Dank, dass du es ansprichst'. (2) Don't minimise. (3) Move forward: 'Lass uns nach vorne schauen'.
german_b2_apologizing_cultural_misunders.register_notes_en:
Cross-cultural apologies carry their own delicate register. (1) FORMAL OR INFORMAL? Depends on the relationship. With a boss or client → 'Sie' + formal phrasing. With a 'du' colleague → still formal apology vocabulary, but 'du'. (2) AVOID 'sorry, sorry, sorry': Germans hear over-apologising as theatrical and insincere. ONE is enough. (3) AVOID self-erasing phrases: 'Sorry, ich bin nur…' reads as weak, not sincere. A CONFIDENT apology: 'Ich habe X getan, das war Y, hätte ich anders gemacht' — full sentences, full accountability. (4) MAKE EYE CONTACT for a face-to-face apology. Looking down reads as insincere in Germany. (5) DON'T REPEAT THE OFFENCE: once you've apologised, don't bring it up five more times.

Formal German apology phrasing:
- 'Es tut mir aufrichtig leid' — strong, sincere
- 'Ich entschuldige mich für…' — formal admission
- 'Bitte verzeihen Sie mir…' — old-fashioned, used for the most formal contexts
- 'Asche auf mein Haupt' (idiom) — playful + formal admission
- 'Reinen Wein einschenken' (idiom) — signals the speaker is about to be honest

When RECEIVING an apology: DO NOT dismiss it with 'Kein Problem' — that invalidates the apology. The right pattern is: 'Vielen Dank, dass du es ansprichst' + 'Lass uns nach vorne schauen'.

Different from many Anglo-American workplaces: a vague, short apology often passes there. In Germany the apology must be structured and specific. Speakers used to the lighter style need to PRACTICE the structured form deliberately.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To be caught off guard — caught at a moment you're not ready. Useful when you need to explain why you reacted badly.
To speak completely frankly — no detours. Signals that you're about to say something difficult but important.
To criticise someone indirectly — hitting A while really aiming at B. Newcomers to German offices sometimes do this without meaning to.

german_b2_international_conference.cultural_notes_en:
International conferences in Germany (Frankfurt Buchmesse, IAA Mobility, drupa, CeBIT-style trade fairs) differ from many Asian and Anglo-American conferences in five ways. (1) FORMAL DRESS CODE: business attire is mandatory for speakers and senior delegates. Casual = read as disrespect for the audience. (2) PRESENTATION STYLE: Germans favour DATA + STRUCTURE over storytelling. Slides carry more text, charts and references than a typical Silicon-Valley deck. Standard pattern: thesis → 3–5 supporting points with data → conclusion + Q&A. (3) Q&A IS THE REAL TEST: German audiences run a tough Q&A — they challenge methodology, sample size, conclusions. DO NOT get defensive. The standard opener is 'Eine sehr gute Frage. Lassen Sie mich das wie folgt einordnen…'. (4) NETWORKING IS THE POINT: 60% of a conference's value lives in the coffee breaks and dinners. Plan ahead: identify 5–10 people you want to meet. DO NOT eat lunch alone; sit at a strangers' table. (5) BUSINESS CARDS ARE SACRED: exchange cards with both hands, read the card before putting it away, and DO NOT scribble notes on it in front of the person who gave it to you.

Different from many Anglo-American or Vietnamese conferences: those tend to have more personal stories and less structured Q&A; German conferences follow a strict academic/business format and the Q&A is central.

Most Vietnamese delegates at German conferences fall into one of three groups: export-focused companies, DAAD-funded researchers, and government delegations. Each group brings different expectations into the cultural setting.

One crucial detail: if you're invited as a SPEAKER, the conference usually covers travel + hotel. If you're an attendee, you pay yourself. Visa: most German conferences will issue an official 'invitation letter' for your visa application.
german_b2_international_conference.tip_advice_en:
Before the conference (4–6 weeks): (1) Register early — early-bird discount + time to prepare. (2) Research speakers and delegates on LinkedIn. (3) Print 50–100 business cards (German + English). (4) If you're a speaker: rehearse 5+ times.

Day 1: (1) Arrive 30–45 minutes EARLY for the first session. (2) Wear business attire. (3) Bring notebook + pen + business cards. (4) Coffee break: introduce yourself proactively. (5) Lunch: sit at a table with strangers. (6) Evening: go to the welcome reception if there is one.

When presenting: (1) Arrive 15 minutes before your session — test mic, projector. (2) Open with an acknowledgement. (3) Speak 20% slower than your normal pace. (4) Interact: 1–2 rhetorical questions to the audience. (5) Q&A: listen to the FULL question before answering. (6) If you don't know the answer: 'Eine sehr berechtigte Frage — die Daten dazu habe ich nicht parat, aber ich folge per E-Mail nach'.

Networking: (1) Have a 30-second elevator pitch ready. (2) Listen 70%, talk 30%. (3) Open questions: 'Was war für Sie das Highlight bisher?'. (4) Card exchange: receive with both hands, read it, brief comment, put it away separately from your wallet. (5) Short note after each meeting.

Follow-up (1–7 days later): (1) Send LinkedIn requests to everyone you met. (2) Follow-up email to your 5–10 priority contacts. (3) If you met a speaker, post a review of their talk on LinkedIn — tag them.
german_b2_international_conference.register_notes_en:
German conferences are formal but not stuffy. (1) ADDRESS: 'Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren' only for large audiences / opening sessions. In Q&A: 'Frau Schulz' / 'Herr Wagner' with last name. In 1-on-1 networking: business cards exchange first, then first names if they offer. (2) PRESENTATION VOCABULARY: use German academic vocabulary — 'These', 'Methodik', 'Ergebnisse', 'Schlussfolgerungen', 'Limitationen'. NO slang or casual fillers. (3) Q&A DEFENCE: the standard opener for every question is 'Eine sehr berechtigte/gute/spannende Frage. Lassen Sie mich das wie folgt einordnen…' — it buys you three seconds of thinking time. (4) ADMIT LIMITATIONS GRACEFULLY: if the data isn't there, 'Diese spezifischen Daten habe ich nicht parat — ich folge per E-Mail nach'. (5) ENGLISH VS GERMAN: at an international conference English is usually the default. But if >50% of the audience is German, switch to German to show effort.

Networking register: small-talk safe topics — your trip, conference highlights, the city. AVOID: politics, religion, personal life (family, salary).

Different from many Anglo-American conferences: those often include personal stories and jokes inside a presentation. In Germany, the presentation is data + structure.

Common mistakes from less experienced delegates: (1) over-thanking — Germans read this as too much; one acknowledgement is enough; (2) under-preparing for Q&A — putting 100% into the talk and forgetting the Q&A is 50% of the impression; (3) shy networking — clustering in the corner with colleagues from home.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To make an impression. In conference context: 'einen guten Eindruck machen' = make a good impression — central for speakers and networking.
To get the ball rolling. Used at the opening of a presentation or panel: 'Lassen Sie mich den Stein ins Rollen bringen' = let me kick things off.

Once committed, follow through to the end. A logic chain: if you accept premise A, you have to accept consequence B. Useful in Q&A.

german_b2_dinner_with_german_guest.cultural_notes_en:
Hosting a German guest for dinner in Vietnam has nuances you need to know. (1) RESTAURANT CHOICE: avoid too touristy, avoid too fine-dining. The sweet spot is mid-range authentic Vietnamese (Quán Bụi, Cục Gạch Quán, Hum Vegetarian) — local but comfortable. (2) MENU NEGOTIATION: DO NOT order for the whole table the way a Vietnamese host normally would. In Germany each person picks their own dish. Suggest 'Wir teilen alle Gerichte' before you order — if the guest is happy with that, fine. (3) SHARING DISHES: if you do share, don't load the guest's plate full for them. Right pattern: order 4–5 dishes for the table, each person serves themselves. (4) DRINKING: Vietnamese beer is weaker than German beer. DO NOT push drinking. DO NOT clink glasses constantly. Toast once at the start, then let the pace go free. (5) PAYING: for a business dinner the company pays. But if the guest insists on 'getrennt zahlen', accept gracefully — don't argue.

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam the host loads the guest's plate (showing care); in Germany you let the guest load their own (showing respect for their autonomy).

FOOD PREFERENCES Germans tend to have: most Germans aren't keen on offal — skip phá lấu and pork intestine dishes. Spice — many Germans aren't used to it; ask first. Vegetarianism: very common in Germany — always offer a vegetarian option. Allergies: gluten and lactose are common — ask in advance.

PHỞ is a safe choice for a first dinner — universally loved, mild, satisfying.

One crucial detail: if the German guest doesn't finish their food, DO NOT push 'ăn nữa đi' (have more). They've had enough. Pressure makes them uncomfortable.
german_b2_dinner_with_german_guest.tip_advice_en:
One week ahead (planning): (1) Ask the guest about dietary preferences/allergies. (2) If it's their first time in Vietnam, pick a comfortable restaurant (English menu, A/C). (3) Make a reservation — Friday/Saturday need 3–5 days' notice.

Dinner night: (1) Arrive 10–15 minutes EARLY. (2) Brief the waiter: 'Wir haben einen Gast aus Deutschland — bitte mild würzen, English menu, Empfehlungen für Anfänger'. (3) When the guest arrives, introduce them to the waiter, seat them where the view is nice if possible. (4) Ask preference: 'Möchten Sie ein Bier oder lieber Tee/Wasser?'.

During dinner: (1) Order 4–5 dishes mixed: 1 noodle (phở), 1 spring roll (gỏi cuốn), 1 grilled, 1 vegetable, 1 rice. (2) When a dish arrives, BRIEFLY explain it. (3) Show how to use chopsticks if the guest is new to them. (4) Toast once at the start. DO NOT clink constantly. (5) Small-talk topics: trip, conference, sightseeing plans — NOT politics, religion, salary, family.

If the guest is struggling with a dish: (1) DO NOT insist. (2) Quietly order an alternative. (3) Offer a fallback: 'Falls heute nicht der richtige Tag ist — morgen können wir auch europäisch essen'.

Paying: (1) Business dinner: signal the waiter discreetly, sign the credit card slip without showing the total. (2) Personal: 'Soll ich heute zahlen oder teilen wir?'.

After dinner: (1) Walk the guest to a Grab/taxi if they're going on alone. (2) The next morning, brief check-in: 'Wie war das Essen gestern? Hat Ihnen alles geschmeckt?'.
german_b2_dinner_with_german_guest.register_notes_en:
A dinner with a German guest sits between formal (still 'Sie') and relaxed (small-talk is more casual than a meeting). (1) STICK WITH 'SIE' throughout a business dinner. Only switch to 'du' if the guest EXPLICITLY offers. (2) FOOD VOCABULARY: learn the German names for Vietnamese dishes — 'Sommerrollen' (gỏi cuốn), 'Rindfleisch-Nudelsuppe' (phở bò). DO NOT make the guest guess. (3) RECOMMENDATIONS, NOT ORDERS: 'Ich empfehle Ihnen…', 'Sehr beliebt ist…', 'Würden Sie probieren…?'. NOT 'Sie müssen das essen'. (4) SMALL-TALK TOPICS: SAFE = trip, conference, sightseeing, food preferences. RISKY = politics, religion, personal salary. AVOID = personal life questions. (5) SILENCES ARE OK: in a German dinner some silence is natural. DO NOT fill every second with chatter.

When the guest orders: DO NOT override their choice. You can gently suggest: 'Eine Alternative wäre…' — then let them decide.

The bill: signal the waiter discreetly. Sign the credit card slip without showing the total. If the guest insists on splitting, accept gracefully.

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam the host usually orders for the whole table; in Germany each person picks their own. In a cross-cultural dinner, ASK first: 'Möchten Sie selbst aussuchen oder soll ich Empfehlungen aussprechen?'.

Common mistakes from less experienced hosts: (1) loading the guest's plate full — reads as controlling; (2) pushing more beer; (3) over-ordering; (4) not briefing the waiter on language preferences.

german_b2_explaining_tet_to_foreigner.cultural_notes_en:
Explaining Tết to a German requires care in bridging cultural distance. (1) ANCHOR TO WEIHNACHTEN: start from the familiar — Christmas. 'Tết ist wie Weihnachten, aber 7 Tage lang und mit der ganzen Großfamilie'. Then add the unique elements (lì xì, bánh chưng, ancestor offerings). (2) KEY CONCEPTS to explain: the lunar calendar, the extended family, ancestor veneration, lì xì, bánh chưng. (3) AVOID OVER-ROMANTICISING: Tết isn't a fairy tale. There's pressure (catching the train home in time, expensive lì xì, the cooking marathon). Honest framing: 'Tết ist wunderschön, aber auch anstrengend — wie Weihnachten in Deutschland mit Verwandten'. (4) DATE CONFUSION: Tết follows the lunar calendar, so dates change. 'Tết fällt zwischen Ende Januar und Mitte Februar'. (5) WORKPLACE IMPACT: with a German colleague, explain that Tết = a 7-day shutdown in Vietnamese business.

Different from a domestic Vietnamese setting: at home Tết is baseline knowledge everyone shares. Abroad you become the cultural translator — you have to explain it in a way that conveys the emotional weight Tết carries for Vietnamese people.

One crucial detail: if a German colleague is genuinely interested, suggest they visit Vietnam during Tết. It's an experience you can't replicate.
german_b2_explaining_tet_to_foreigner.tip_advice_en:
When you explain Tết: (1) STORYTELLING > academic. A 2–3 minute personal story beats a Wikipedia summary. (2) VISUALS HELP: show photos on your phone — Tết altar, hoa đào/mai blossoms, red envelopes. (3) FOOD ANGLE: Germans appreciate food. Mention bánh chưng, bánh tét, mứt, nem chua. If possible, let them try some. (4) GIFTS IF APPROPRIATE: if a colleague has a strong connection to Tết culture, a small box of mứt is a nice touch. (5) WORKPLACE PREP: a month before Tết, send an email to German colleagues about the office closure.

Common questions Germans ask:
- 'Warum so wichtig?' → Family + ancestors + new year + spring + community in one
- 'Wann genau?' → Lunar calendar, late January to mid-February
- 'Was esst ihr?' → Bánh Chưng, mứt, gà luộc, xôi, dưa hành
- 'Was schenkt man?' → Lì xì for kids/elders, fruit baskets for hosts
- 'Was ist tabu?' → Sweeping the house on day 1, breaking things, crying

If the colleague is invited to a family Tết in Vietnam, brief them on:
- Bring a small gift (fruit basket, sweets)
- Greet the elders first ('Chúc mừng năm mới ạ')
- Don't refuse food (rude); take a small portion if you don't like it
- Lì xì for the kids (small amount)
- Dress nicely (red is auspicious, white is to be avoided)
german_b2_explaining_tet_to_foreigner.register_notes_en:
Explaining Tết = personal storytelling + cultural context. (1) USE 'WIR' framing: 'Wir Vietnamesen feiern Tết so…'. It signals an insider perspective. (2) ANALOGIES with Weihnachten are OK but DO NOT over-equate. 'Tết ist wie Weihnachten, aber…' — make the difference explicit. (3) PROPER NOUNS: keep the original Vietnamese names in German ('Bánh Chưng' rather than only 'Reiskuchen'; 'Tết' rather than only 'vietnamesisches Neujahr'). (4) AVOID OVER-DRAMATISING: Tết is wonderful but it has its downsides. Honest framing > fairy tale. (5) ENGAGE WITH QUESTIONS: if a German asks a 'naive' question, DO NOT get defensive.

When inviting a German guest to join Tết: register is slightly more formal if it's your boss ('Es wäre mir eine Ehre, wenn Sie unser Tết-Fest miterleben würden'). More casual with a close colleague ('Komm doch zu uns Tết feiern!').

Different from a Vietnamese setting: at home Tết is common knowledge — you don't have to explain. Abroad you're a cultural educator — practise explaining it succinctly and engagingly.

Common mistakes from less experienced explainers: (1) over-explain (a 5-minute lecture on 4,000 years of history) — Germans bore quickly; (2) under-explain (dismiss with 'It's like Christmas') — miss the richness; (3) apologise for 'old-fashioned' aspects — nothing to apologise for.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: The most important festival, the pre-eminent one. A grand, sweeping phrase — useful when you want to convey to a German listener how much emotional weight Tết carries.
To preserve tradition rather than let it fade. Useful when explaining ancient practices (the altar, lì xì) — it signals intentional preservation.

german_b2_cultural_clash_conversation.cultural_notes_en:
A difficult cross-cultural conversation needs careful preparation. (1) TIMING + LOCATION: NOT in the open-plan workplace. NOT after hours when both of you are tired. Best: a café near the office at lunchtime, or a small meeting room with the door closed. (2) AGENDA-DRIVEN but EMPATHETIC: open by framing the purpose — DO NOT attack. 'Stefan, ich möchte gerne über unsere Zusammenarbeit der letzten Wochen sprechen — was gut läuft und wo wir besser werden können'. (3) USE 'I-STATEMENTS': 'Ich habe mich gefühlt…' rather than 'Du hast mich verletzt'. I-statements are harder to argue with. (4) SEPARATE BEHAVIOUR FROM PERSON: 'Dein Verhalten in dem Meeting hat mich getroffen' — not 'Du bist unsensibel'. That distinction is the core skill. (5) END FORWARD-LOOKING: DO NOT close by dwelling on the past. Close with 'Wie können wir besser zusammenarbeiten?'.

Different from many Vietnamese (and some East Asian) settings: there conflict is often avoided or handled through an intermediary. In Germany, a direct face-to-face conversation with the person involved is what's expected. People used to the indirect style need to practise confronting directly — uncomfortable but necessary.

In German subsidiaries in Vietnam, HR usually has a written policy for workplace conflict resolution — typically 1-on-1 first, escalate to the manager if needed, then HR.

One crucial detail: if the conversation goes off the rails (escalates, gets emotional), it's OK to pause. 'Stefan, ich merke, dass dieses Gespräch gerade emotional wird — lass uns morgen weitermachen'. A pause is strength, not weakness.
german_b2_cultural_clash_conversation.tip_advice_en:
Before the meeting: (1) WRITE DOWN the issues you want to discuss. Specific, not vague. (2) RECOGNISE YOUR OWN ROLE. It's rarely 100% one side's fault. The right move: 'Vielleicht habe auch ich nicht klar genug kommuniziert'. (3) RESEARCH the cultural context.

During the meeting: (1) OPEN: 'Hast du fünf Minuten? Ich möchte etwas Wichtiges besprechen'. (2) STATE PURPOSE. (3) GIVE A SPECIFIC EXAMPLE: 1–2 concrete incidents, not 5+. (4) DESCRIBE IMPACT: 'Das hat mich Y empfinden lassen'. NOT 'You should…'. (5) LISTEN to the response. (6) ACKNOWLEDGE their perspective: 'Ich verstehe deine Sicht'. (7) PROPOSE a way forward.

Standard phrasing:
- 'Wir reden aneinander vorbei' (idiom)
- 'Es war nicht meine Absicht' — clarify intent
- 'Lass uns Tabula rasa machen' (idiom)
- 'Andere Länder, andere Sitten' (idiom)
- 'Wie können wir besser zusammenarbeiten?'

Avoid:
- Bringing up 5 grievances at once
- 'Always' / 'never'
- Comparing to other colleagues
- Threatening escalation
- Crying or raising your voice

After the meeting: (1) CONFIRM key takeaways in writing. (2) FOLLOW THROUGH. (3) CHECK IN after two weeks.
german_b2_cultural_clash_conversation.register_notes_en:
A difficult cross-cultural conversation calls for a SPECIAL REGISTER. (1) MORE FORMAL than usual: even with a 'du' colleague, the sentence structure is more formal — full sentences, careful word choice. (2) NEUTRAL VOCABULARY: avoid emotionally charged words. 'Ich habe mich gemaßregelt gefühlt' > 'Du hast mich gedemütigt'. (3) HEDGING phrases: 'Vielleicht…', 'Mein Eindruck war…', 'Ich kann mich auch täuschen, aber…' — they signal you're open to another interpretation. (4) PAUSES ARE OK: difficult conversations naturally have silences. DO NOT fill every gap with chatter. (5) AVOID HUMOUR: jokes can read as minimising.

Standard opening/closing:
- Opening: 'Hast du Zeit für ein offenes Gespräch?'
- Framing: 'Ich möchte etwas ansprechen, das mich beschäftigt'
- Acknowledge: 'Ich verstehe deine Sicht'
- Forward: 'Wie können wir besser zusammenarbeiten?'
- Closing: 'Vielen Dank für das offene Gespräch'

When RECEIVING criticism from a German colleague, the pattern is: (1) thank them for raising it, (2) listen fully, (3) acknowledge their perspective, (4) ask clarifying questions, (5) take time to respond if needed, (6) propose action.

Different from many indirect-communication cultures: there, face-to-face conflicts are usually avoided. In Germany, face-to-face is expected.

Common mistakes: (1) avoiding the conversation entirely; (2) raising it by email; (3) escalating to HR / manager too quickly; (4) over-apologising; (5) crying / getting emotional.

To accidentally offend someone (literally: 'to step on someone's tie'). Useful when you want to reference a past offence without dramatising it.
To wipe the slate clean and start fresh. Useful when a difficult conversation ends on a positive note.
Different countries, different customs. A frame for invoking cultural difference without passing judgement.

german_b2_building_friendship_foreigner.cultural_notes_en:
Building a friendship with a German in Vietnam follows different rules than friendship with Vietnamese people. (1) FRIENDSHIP TAKES TIME in Germany: Germans strictly distinguish 'Bekanntschaft' (acquaintance) from 'Freundschaft' (friendship). 'Freundschaft' is built over months and years. DO NOT expect a German to call you 'Freund' after one round of beers. (2) PRIVACY IS SACRED: Germans are very private. DO NOT ask about salary, family plans, religion, politics early on. Safe topics: hobbies, travel, food, sports, work projects. (3) CONSISTENCY > INTENSITY: a weekly 30-minute coffee for 6 months > one expensive dinner. Germans trust people who show up regularly. (4) RECIPROCITY: if they invite you, return an invite at a similar scale. DO NOT over-give. (5) PERSONAL SPACE: even with close friends, hugging is less common in Germany than in Vietnam.

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam friendship can form quickly through shared food + drinks. In Germany it's slower but deeper once it's established. Patience is required.

In the expat scene in Vietnam, German expats often cluster together. Sometimes it feels hard to break in. Tip: don't approach them as a 'tourist' — approach them as a fellow professional / local with shared interests.

One crucial detail: if a friendship goes deep, a German may switch to 'du' with you — that's a MEANINGFUL transition, not a casual one.
german_b2_building_friendship_foreigner.tip_advice_en:
Initiating friendship: (1) START LOW-PRESSURE: coffee, lunch, walk — short commitment. (2) SHARED INTEREST: identify 1 common piece of ground. (3) BE PATIENT: if they decline the first time, don't take it personally. (4) RECIPROCITY: balance giving and receiving.

Deepening friendship: (1) CONSISTENCY: weekly run, monthly dinner. (2) HELP IN SMALL WAYS: if they're struggling with Vietnamese bureaucracy, offer practical help. (3) REMEMBER DETAILS: birthday, important dates. (4) BE HONEST: Germans value directness.

When they reciprocate: (1) ACCEPT invitations. (2) ASK QUESTIONS about German culture. (3) LEARN basic German phrases for casual settings.

Maintaining a long-distance friendship: (1) WhatsApp regularly but not daily. (2) Send Vietnam updates. (3) Visit when you're in Germany. (4) Welcome them back to Vietnam.

Standard phrasing:
- 'Lust auf…?' — casual invitation
- 'Magst du mit?' — group invitation
- 'Wir könnten mal…' — soft suggestion
- 'Bei mir kannst du jederzeit…' — open availability

Avoid:
- Over-sharing early
- Expecting them to adapt 100% to Vietnamese style
- Taking silence/decline personally
- Pressing for a label
german_b2_building_friendship_foreigner.register_notes_en:
Becoming friends with a German involves subtle register shifts. (1) START WITH 'SIE': in a workplace context, even with a close colleague, 'Sie' is the default. Switch to 'du' when: (a) they propose it, (b) the social context is outside work, (c) startup/agency culture. (2) 'DU' = MEANINGFUL: if they offer 'du', that's an intimacy upgrade. Accept gracefully. (3) DEPTH STAGES: Stage 1 small-talk (weather, sport, food); Stage 2 personal interests (hobbies, travel); Stage 3 vulnerable topics (work struggles, family). Don't skip stages. (4) HUMOUR EVOLVES: early friendship — safe humour (observational, self-deprecating). Established friendship — sarcasm, German dry wit. (5) PRIVACY is respected.

Standard phrasing by stage:
- Stage 1 (early): 'Lust auf einen Kaffee?'
- Stage 2 (developing): 'Hast du am Wochenende was vor?'
- Stage 3 (close): 'Bei mir kannst du jederzeit vorbeikommen'

When a German friend shares emotional content (rare): LISTEN, don't try to fix it.

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam friendship can be high-touch. In Germany a healthy friendship has space — weekly contact, monthly meetings = a normal close friendship.

Common mistakes: (1) over-communicating early; (2) expecting them available 24/7; (3) reading silence as rejection; (4) pushing for a label; (5) under-communicating after they leave Vietnam.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To jump over your own shadow — to overcome yourself, to do something against your own nature. In cross-cultural friendship: both sides sometimes have to 'über den eigenen Schatten springen'.
To become friends with someone — describes the gradual process, not an event. Germans use this verb to describe how a friendship develops.
To be on the same wavelength — to communicate easily, share humour, share values. The phrase for the moment a friendship really clicks.

german_b2_immigration_border_officer.cultural_notes_en:
Going through German border control (Bundespolizei) for the first time is a sensitive moment — one wrong detail can get you held for an extra 2–3 hours. Five core points for Vietnamese travellers. (1) DOCUMENTS READY IN HAND: passport + visa + employment letter (Arbeitsvertrag) + proof of address (Anmeldebestätigung or hotel booking) + return ticket (if any). Have them ready BEFORE you reach the counter — don't dig through your bag at the booth. (2) LANGUAGE: prefer GERMAN. Try to say 'Guten Tag' and open in German — border officers respond noticeably better. If you don't understand, switch to English: 'Entschuldigung, könnten wir auf Englisch sprechen?'. (3) ANSWERS SHORT AND DIRECT: 'Wie lange bleiben Sie?' → 'Zwei Jahre, mit gültigem Arbeitsvisum'. NO personal stories, NO jokes about 'Drogen', 'Waffen', 'illegal'. (4) DON'T OPEN YOUR LUGGAGE PROACTIVELY: only open it when the officer asks. Opening it first looks suspicious. (5) CASH > EUR 10,000: must be DECLARED. Failing to declare = heavy fine + possible confiscation.

Different from Vietnamese norms: at Vietnamese border control officers are often friendly and chatty. At German/Schengen control it's factual, short, professional. Don't expect small-talk.

One crucial detail: if it's your first work visa (D-Visum, 90 days), you'll need to register your address (Anmeldung) within 14 days of arrival and apply for the Aufenthaltstitel at the Ausländerbehörde within 90 days. The border officer does NOT issue this — they only stamp your entry date.

At Frankfurt and Munich there are separate lanes for EU citizens — you queue at 'All Passports / Non-EU'. Wait times at peak hours: 30–90 minutes. Plan accordingly.
german_b2_immigration_border_officer.tip_advice_en:
Before the flight (1 week ahead): (1) Print EVERY document on paper: visa, Arbeitsvertrag, Anmeldebestätigung/booking, return ticket, proof of finances (Sperrkonto, bank statement). PDF on your phone is not enough — Germany expects paper. (2) Write your temporary address on a separate slip (street, Hausnummer, PLZ) — the officer may ask for it. (3) Optionally download the Bundespolizei app to know the procedure.

At the counter: (1) Stand upright, alone (not in a group). (2) Put passport + visa OPEN ON THE VISA PAGE on the counter. (3) Say 'Guten Tag' when the officer looks up. (4) Answer questions SHORTLY, don't elaborate. (5) If you don't understand, politely ask again: 'Könnten Sie das wiederholen?'.

Standard answers to the 5 common questions:
- 'Was ist der Zweck Ihres Aufenthalts?' → 'Arbeit / Studium / Tourismus'
- 'Wie lange bleiben Sie?' → 'Zwei Jahre, mit gültigem Arbeitsvisum'
- 'Wo werden Sie wohnen?' → '[specific address]'
- 'Wer ist Ihr Arbeitgeber?' → 'Bosch GmbH in Stuttgart'
- 'Haben Sie etwas zu verzollen?' → 'Nein, nichts zu verzollen' (if true)

DO NOT: (1) Say 'I don't know' about your address / employer — you have to know; (2) Open your phone to show personal photos; (3) Argue if held for further inspection — comply, and call your consulate if needed; (4) Try to bribe — a serious crime in Germany.

If held for secondary inspection: (1) Stay calm, cooperate. (2) Request an interpreter if you don't understand: 'Ich brauche einen Dolmetscher, bitte'. (3) DO NOT sign anything you don't understand. (4) Contact the Vietnamese Embassy in Berlin: +49 30 53630108 (24/7 emergency line).
german_b2_immigration_border_officer.register_notes_en:
German border control is absolutely formal. (1) ALWAYS 'SIE' — the officer never uses 'du'. Your answer is also 'Sie': 'Ja, hier ist mein Pass' (NOT 'Hier hast du'). (2) SHORT, FACTUAL TONE: a 5–10-word answer beats a 30-word one. 'Arbeit. Zwei Jahre' is enough; 'I am coming to Germany long-term to develop my career…' = too long. (3) DON'T JOKE: jokes about drugs, weapons, illegal status can trigger a 2–3-hour secondary inspection. Officers are trained to spot evasion, not appreciate humour. (4) MEDICAL/LEGAL VOCABULARY: use formal terms — 'Reisepass' (not 'Pass'), 'Aufenthalt' (not 'Bleibe'), 'Arbeitgeber' (not 'Chef'). (5) POLITELY ASK AGAIN: if you didn't understand, 'Könnten Sie das wiederholen?' or 'Entschuldigung, ich habe nicht verstanden'. DO NOT nod silently if you don't understand — that reads as evasion.

Standard phrasing for each question type:
- Purpose: 'Arbeit / Tourismus / Studium / Familie'
- Duration: 'Zwei Jahre' / 'Drei Wochen' / 'Sechs Monate'
- Address: full address with PLZ (postcode)
- Money: exact figure in euros
- Declaration: 'Nein, nichts zu verzollen' or 'Ja, ich möchte X verzollen'

Different from many Anglo-American settings: there you can chat lightly with the officer ('How's your day?'). At German control: zero small-talk. Wait for the officer to greet you, answer, wait for the next question.

Common mistakes from less experienced travellers: (1) over-explain — giving information the officer didn't ask for; (2) American-style 'Hi, how are you?' — the German officer expects formal 'Guten Tag'; (3) arguing if questioned — comply, don't argue.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To play it safe — go with the safest option, don't take risks. In a border context: 'Ich gehe auf Nummer sicher und nehme alle Dokumente in Papierform mit' = I'm playing it safe and bringing all documents on paper.
To make a clean slate — declare everything honestly, put it all on the table. In a customs context: if you have something to declare, declare it up front; don't wait for the officer to find it.

german_b2_lost_passport_embassy.cultural_notes_en:
Losing your passport in Germany is a serious emergency — the Vietnamese Embassy in Berlin (Elsenstraße 3, 12435 Berlin) is the rescue station. Five core points. (1) FILE THE POLICE REPORT FIRST: as soon as you discover it's lost, go to the nearest Polizeiwache and file an Anzeige. The embassy WILL ask for this paper — without it you'll be sent back. (2) LIMITED OPENING HOURS: the embassy is open Mon–Fri, 9–12 only. Get there by 8:30 to queue. Weekends or German/Vietnamese holidays = closed. (3) NOTPASS vs. FULL PASSPORT: a Notpass (emergency passport) is issued in 1–3 working days, valid for one year, and only usable to fly back to Vietnam. A regular passport takes 4–6 weeks. In an emergency, apply for the Notpass. (4) FEES: about EUR 50–100 for the Notpass + ~EUR 25 for photos + a rush surcharge in some cases. Pay in cash, no card. (5) LANGUAGE: embassy staff speak Vietnamese — you don't need German there. But the Anzeige from the German police is in German.

Different from many Vietnamese settings: at home you can sometimes have relatives handle paperwork remotely for you. In Germany the embassy requires YOUR personal presence — nobody can do it on your behalf.

Vietnamese Embassy Berlin emergency hotline: +49 30 53630108. Reachable 24/7 for genuine emergencies (lost documents + stranded at the airport, etc.).

If your German visa was lost together with the passport: you have to re-apply for the Aufenthaltstitel at the Ausländerbehörde in your German city of residence — a separate process from the Vietnamese Notpass. One document does not cover both.

One crucial detail: keep photocopies of your passport + visa in the cloud (Google Drive / iCloud) — not just on your phone (your phone can be lost too). Before your trip, scan + upload.
german_b2_lost_passport_embassy.tip_advice_en:
Before the trip (preparation): (1) Photocopy your passport + visa 3 times: 1 carry separately (not in the same bag as the original), 1 with family in Vietnam, 1 uploaded to the cloud. (2) Save in your phone: the Berlin embassy hotline (+49 30 53630108), the embassy address (Elsenstraße 3, 12435 Berlin), and the passport-insurance number if you have one. (3) Buy travel insurance that covers lost documents.

When you discover it's lost (emergency timeline): (1) First, search again — bag, luggage, taxi seat, hotel. Many 'lost' passports are actually misplaced. (2) Within 2 hours: get to the nearest Polizeiwache (or Bundespolizei if you're at an airport). Bring a backup ID (driver's licence, passport copy). Request the Anzeige — the official report. (3) Within 24 hours: call the Vietnamese Embassy in Berlin to confirm opening hours. (4) Next working day: go to the embassy with: copy of the old passport, the Anzeige, 4 4×6 photos (white background, recent), your Aufenthaltstitel (German visa), EUR 100 in cash.

At the embassy: (1) Take a number ticket. (2) Fill in the Notpass application form. (3) Submit your documents at the counter. (4) Staff conducts a quick interview: name, date of birth, reason for loss, intended departure date. (5) Get a receipt with the pickup date for the Notpass.

While waiting for the Notpass: (1) Don't travel far from the city — you may be asked to come back quickly. (2) If you have a flight booked while your old visa is gone, RESCHEDULE to a day after you receive the Notpass. (3) Contact your company's HR (if you're working) — they can help.

Questions to ask the embassy officer: 'When can I pick up the Notpass?', 'Do I need to come back to sign?', 'Is there any way to expedite further?', 'Do I need a new visa for the Notpass to fly back to Vietnam?', 'Where do I get a new full passport once I'm back in Vietnam?'.

Final tip: if you lose your passport during a German holiday period (Karneval, Weihnachten), the embassy may be closed. Plan: wait for the next working day + you may need to stay in Germany 1–2 days beyond your plan. Inform your company / airline.
german_b2_lost_passport_embassy.register_notes_en:
At the Vietnamese Embassy in Berlin, the register is in VIETNAMESE — formal and polite because this is a state agency. Use age-appropriate Vietnamese honorifics. DO NOT speak German even if the officer knows it — they're there to serve Vietnamese citizens in their mother tongue.

When you MUST use German:
- At the Polizeiwache (filing the Anzeige) — all in formal German
- When calling the airline to confirm the Notpass — German or English
- At the Ausländerbehörde for a new Aufenthaltstitel — formal German

Formal German for border/police:
- 'Ich möchte einen verlorenen Reisepass melden' (I'd like to report a lost passport)
- 'Ich möchte Anzeige erstatten' (I'd like to file a police report)
- 'Bitte stellen Sie eine Bescheinigung aus' (Please issue me a certificate)
- 'Wann kann ich die Bescheinigung abholen?' (When can I collect the certificate?)

One crucial detail: at the Polizeiwache the officers are GERMAN — they don't speak Vietnamese. You need German at B2 or you need to bring a translator. If you're not confident, request 'Ich brauche einen Dolmetscher' (I need an interpreter) — they'll schedule one (possibly a 1–2 hour wait).

Common mistakes from less experienced travellers: (1) panicking and speaking too fast — German officers can't follow; (2) bringing too few documents — sent back; (3) being uncertain about the timeline — Notpass really is express in 24–48h, no need to worry.

vocabulary.pronunciation_en: AHN-tsy-guh air-SHTAH-ten — to file a police report
dee OON-ter-lah-gen EYE-n-ry-khen — to submit documents

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To help someone out of a tight spot. The embassy literally 'hilft aus der Patsche' when a traveller has lost their documents. A warm phrase, used to thank someone for a real rescue.
To get away with just a fright — to escape a bad situation with minimal damage. Fits cases where you lose your passport but get a Notpass in time and don't miss your flight.
At the very last minute. Describes losing your passport close to the departure date: 'Auf den letzten Drücker den Notpass bekommen' = picked up the Notpass at the last minute.

To keep your head — stay calm, don't panic. The standard advice for emergencies (lost passport, theft): panic = bad decisions. 'Bei Verstand bleiben und systematisch vorgehen' = stay calm and proceed systematically.

german_b2_deutsche_bahn_ticket_change.cultural_notes_en:
Deutsche Bahn (DB) runs a huge network and is regularly late — Germany is not as famously punctual on rail as the stereotype suggests. About 30% of trains run >6 minutes late. Five core points for Vietnamese travellers. (1) PASSENGER RIGHTS: under EU Fahrgastrechte, if your train is >60 minutes late you're entitled to 25% of the fare back; >120 minutes = 50%. CANCELLED train = free rebooking OR full refund. You have to claim via the DB Navigator app or an online form. (2) AUTOMATIC vs. MANUAL: some compensation is automatic (especially for registered BahnCard holders), but most you have to claim. Don't wait for DB to act on its own. (3) REBOOKING FEES: a Sparpreis ticket has a EUR 19 change fee; a Flexpreis ticket changes for free. If the fault is DB's (cancellation / major delay), BOTH types can be changed free. (4) ENGLISH SUPPORT: counter staff at major stations (Hauptbahnhof) speak English; at small stations only German. If your German is weak, go to a large station. (5) DOCUMENTATION: screenshot the delay info from the DB Navigator app — that's evidence for any dispute. Keep your boarding pass + email confirmation.

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam, when buses or trains run late, there's usually no compensation system. In Germany the legal system is explicit — staff are NOT allowed to refuse if you have a legal entitlement. But they may not proactively offer; you have to know your rights and assert them.

At DB counters staff occasionally PUSH BACK on legitimate claims — not out of bad faith, but because the policies are complex and they avoid exceptions. Pattern: counter rep refuses → you request a Vorgesetzte (supervisor) → 70% get approved. Don't give up.

One crucial detail: if you miss an Anschluss (connection) because of an upstream delay, DB has to provide an alternative free — even when the alternative is a pricier express. That's the 'Mobilitätsgarantie'.
german_b2_deutsche_bahn_ticket_change.tip_advice_en:
Before you go to the counter (preparation): (1) Open the DB Navigator app — screenshot the page showing the delay/cancellation. That's your main evidence. (2) Have your ticket + email confirmation ready. (3) If you missed an Anschluss, note the scheduled arrival time + actual arrival time — calculate the delay precisely.

At the counter (standard script): (1) 'Guten Tag, ich möchte mein Ticket umbuchen wegen Zugausfall'. (2) Hand over ticket + screenshot. (3) Wait while the agent checks the system. (4) If they say 'Es kostet 19 Euro' → reply: 'Laut Beförderungsbedingungen habe ich bei Zugausfall Anspruch auf kostenlose Umbuchung'. (5) If they still refuse → 'Könnten Sie das mit Ihrer Vorgesetzten klären?' — DO NOT argue, just escalate. (6) If the supervisor also refuses → ask for a written reason: 'Bitte begründen Sie das schriftlich' — 80% will approve when they hear this (nobody wants a paper trail).

Assertive but polite phrasing:
- 'Ich verstehe — aber laut Fahrgastrechten…' (I understand — but under passenger rights…)
- 'Könnten Sie mir die rechtliche Grundlage zeigen?' (Could you show me the legal basis?)
- 'Ich möchte das schriftlich' (I'd like that in writing)
- 'Wer ist für Beschwerden zuständig?' (Who's responsible for complaints?)

Avoid:
- Yelling — Germans treat raised voices as harassment; you can be asked to leave
- 'In Vietnam würden wir…' — irrelevant, weakens your position
- Crying — doesn't help, embarrasses both sides
- 'I'll sue' — empty threat, undermines credibility

If you really are refused at the counter: (1) Keep your ticket + screenshot. (2) Take the alternative train — you may need to buy a new ticket (out of pocket for now). (3) After the trip, claim a refund via the DB online form: bahn.de/fahrgastrechte. (4) Either post or online submission. Processing time: 4–8 weeks.

One crucial detail: if you hold a BahnCard 25/50/100, the claim process is more automatic — DB has your registration data. Without one, attach a copy of your ID when you claim.

Tip for newcomers in Germany: install the apps 'DB Navigator' + 'Trainline' (alternative). Both show real-time delay info and push notifications when your train is delayed or cancelled.
german_b2_deutsche_bahn_ticket_change.register_notes_en:
At a DB counter / with a conductor / on the DB hotline, the register is ASSERTIVE FORMAL — you're asserting rights but not hostile. (1) 'SIE' always — DB staff never 'du'. (2) RIGHTS LANGUAGE: 'Anspruch auf', 'laut Beförderungsbedingungen', 'gemäß Fahrgastrechten' — these signal you know the law. Staff push back less when they hear legal terminology. (3) POLITE ESCALATION: 'Könnten Sie das bitte mit Ihrer Vorgesetzten klären?' = formal escalation. NOT 'Lass mich mit dem Manager sprechen' (let me talk to the manager) — too American-style, alienates. (4) DOCUMENT REQUEST: 'Ich möchte das schriftlich' (I want that in writing) — a formal request for written reasoning. Powerful tool — staff don't want a paper trail behind a refusal and will often approve immediately. (5) BLAME LANGUAGE: avoid 'Ihre Schuld' (your fault) — accusatory, puts staff on the defensive. Use impersonal language: 'Die Verspätung liegt nicht bei mir' (the delay isn't on my side). Frame the issue, not the person.

Standard phrasing for a dispute:
- 'Ich verstehe — aber laut Beförderungsbedingungen…' (I understand — but under the transport conditions…)
- 'Welche rechtliche Grundlage haben Sie dafür?' (What legal basis do you have for that?)
- 'Bitte begründen Sie die Ablehnung schriftlich' (Please justify the refusal in writing)
- 'Wer ist für Beschwerden zuständig?' (Who handles complaints?)

When you have to ACCEPT a loss: 'Ich akzeptiere das jetzt — werde aber online über bahn.de/fahrgastrechte claimen' (I'll accept it for now — but I'll claim online).

Different from Vietnamese norms: in Vietnam staff disputes are usually resolved via relationship / personal connection. In Germany they're resolved via RIGHTS + DOCUMENTATION. A personal appeal ('I'm a foreigner, please help') rarely works; a legal appeal ('I have a right to X') often does.

Common mistakes from less experienced travellers: (1) accepting the first refusal — losing money for nothing; (2) yelling — counterproductive in Germany; (3) missing the claim deadline (60 days from the date of travel) — lost forever; (4) not screenshotting evidence — no document = no claim.

dair AHN-shprookh owf — right/claim to something

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To be right and to be granted you're right — being legally correct doesn't automatically win the argument; you have to assert and escalate. Useful when DB refuses a legitimate claim.

To dig in and refuse to budge. Used to describe a DB agent who refuses every argument. You can then say: 'Wenn der Schalter auf stur schaltet, eskalieren Sie zur Vorgesetzten' (when the agent digs in, escalate to the supervisor).
To draw the short straw — to come out the loser in a dispute. If you don't assert your rights, you 'ziehen den Kürzeren'. A useful warning to yourself: you have to push, or you end up out of pocket.

To bite into the sour apple — bite the bullet, accept the unfavourable outcome when the alternative is worse. In a DB context: accept the EUR 19 rebooking fee if you don't have time to fight, then claim it back online.

german_b2_hospital_emergency_visit.cultural_notes_en:
The German healthcare system differs from many others in five ways. (1) NOTAUFNAHME = ER, NOT WALK-IN: only go to a Notaufnahme if it's TRULY URGENT (severe pain, accident, difficulty breathing). Not urgent → go to your Hausarzt (family doctor) or a Bereitschaftspraxis (out-of-hours practice). Going to the Notaufnahme for a cold = a 4–6 hour wait + an unhappy staff. (2) INSURANCE CARD MANDATORY: you need a German insurance card (TK, AOK, Barmer, or private). International travel insurance — Reise-Krankenversicherung — only covers urgent care, not routine. (3) NO PAYMENT ON THE SPOT: with statutory insurance (gesetzliche Versicherung) you DO NOT pay anything at the Notaufnahme — it all goes through the card. There may be a Praxisgebühr of EUR 10 (abolished in 2013 but reactivated in some Bundesländer in 2026 — verify). Private insurance: you pay up front, claim back. (4) WAIT TIMES: the Notaufnahme runs Triage — serious cases get priority. Mild abdominal pain can wait 3–5 hours. Chest pain + shortness of breath = seen immediately. (5) LANGUAGE: ER doctors usually speak English in big cities (Berlin, Munich, Hamburg). If you're worried about communication, bring a translator or use Google Translate for symptoms.

Different from many other systems: in Vietnam you can walk into an ER any time and pay at the counter. In Germany the process is structured and there's a 'system'. Walk-ins for non-emergencies = sent away or kept waiting for a very long time.

One crucial detail: if you're ill but not urgent, call 116 117 (Bereitschaftsdienst — backup doctor service) — they'll direct you to the nearest suitable place. Save this number.

The Hausarzt is your primary doctor in Germany. Register with a Hausarzt when you arrive + go regularly. The Hausarzt provides referrals to specialists, prescribes medication, and writes the Krankschreibung (sick note for your employer).
german_b2_hospital_emergency_visit.tip_advice_en:
Before you go to the Notaufnahme: (1) Self-assess the urgency. Mild abdominal pain only — DO NOT use the Notaufnahme. Call 116 117. If life-threatening — call 112 (ambulance). (2) Bring: Versicherungskarte (yellow/green card), passport/Aufenthaltstitel, list of current medications, list of allergies (if any). (3) Charge your phone — you may wait several hours.

At reception (Anmeldung): (1) 'Guten Tag, ich brauche eine Notaufnahme'. (2) Hand over your Versicherungskarte. (3) Describe your symptoms briefly — the staff aren't doctors, they just register you. (4) Take a wait number.

When the doctor calls your name: (1) 'Guten Tag, Frau/Herr Doktor'. (2) Describe symptoms in order: WHEN IT STARTED + WHERE IT HURTS + HOW IT HURTS + WHAT OTHER SYMPTOMS. (3) Answer medical questions — the doctor will ask: allergies, current medications, medical history, family history. (4) If you don't understand a German medical term, ASK: 'Was bedeutet [word] genau?'.

Basic German medical phrasing:
- 'Ich habe Schmerzen' (I'm in pain)
- 'Es tut weh, wenn ich [verb]' (it hurts when I [verb])
- 'Skala 1–10' (1–10 scale): the doctor will ask the pain level
- 'Allergisch gegen X' (allergic to X)
- 'Ich nehme regelmäßig X ein' (I take X regularly)
- 'Mein Hausarzt ist Dr. Y' (my family doctor is)

When you get a prescription (Rezept): (1) Read it carefully — verify the drug name, dose, instructions. (2) Ask if it interacts with anything else you take. (3) Take the Rezept to the nearest Apotheke (pharmacy). (4) The pharmacist will hand over the medication + explain usage. (5) Statutory insurance covers most of it — you pay a Zuzahlung of EUR 5–10.

Krankschreibung (sick note): (1) An ER doctor can write 1–3 days max. (2) For longer, see your Hausarzt. (3) Submit to your employer within 3 days. (4) In Germany you DO NOT have to disclose the diagnosis to your employer — only the AU (Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung) certificate. Privacy is strict.

Final tip: if your German is not yet B2 and you're seriously ill, go to a university-hospital Notaufnahme (Charité Berlin, Klinikum München) — younger staff + better English.
german_b2_hospital_emergency_visit.register_notes_en:
At a Notaufnahme/Hausarzt, the register is FORMAL but CLEAR. German doctors dislike vague symptoms. (1) 'SIE' with the doctor + staff — always formal. (2) MEDICAL VOCABULARY: use the technical term if you know it, not 'Bauchweh' (informal) but 'Bauchschmerzen' (formal). 'Übelkeit' rather than 'mir ist schlecht'. (3) DESCRIBE SYMPTOMS in structure: WHEN STARTED + WHERE + INTENSITY + ACCOMPANYING. Pattern: 'Seit [time] habe ich [symptom] in [location], Skala [1–10], außerdem [secondary symptom]'. (4) ASK FOR CONFIRMATION: 'Verstehe ich richtig — Sie verschreiben mir [drug]?' (Do I understand correctly — you're prescribing me [drug]?). Don't assume. (5) CULTURAL NOTE: German doctors have LESS bedside manner than US doctors — short, factual, no 'How are you feeling?' empathy. Don't read that as rudeness. They focus on diagnosis.

Questions doctors typically ask (prepare answers in advance):
- 'Wann haben die Beschwerden begonnen?' (when did the symptoms start)
- 'Wo genau tut es weh?' (exactly where does it hurt)
- 'Wie stark sind die Schmerzen, Skala 1–10?' (pain level)
- 'Haben Sie Fieber gemessen?' (have you measured the fever)
- 'Allergien?' (allergies?)
- 'Welche Medikamente nehmen Sie?' (what medications are you taking?)
- 'Vorerkrankungen?' (pre-existing conditions?)
- 'Sind Sie krankenversichert?' (do you have health insurance?)

Assertive phrasing when needed:
- 'Bitte bestätigen Sie schriftlich, dass…' (please confirm in writing that…)
- 'Ich brauche eine zweite Meinung' (I need a second opinion)
- 'Welche Alternativen gibt es?' (what alternatives are there?)

Different from many other systems: in Vietnam you may chat informally with the doctor and expect emotional support. In Germany the doctor focuses on diagnosis/treatment; emotional support is up to you and your family. Don't expect emotional comfort from the doctor.

Common mistakes from less experienced patients: (1) underestimating severity — 'it's nothing' until it's worse; (2) embarrassment about symptoms (especially gynaecological, intestinal) — German doctors treat these as normal medical info; (3) accepting a prescription without asking about side effects.

idiom_glosses.meaning_en: To grit your teeth and bear it — bite the bullet. In medical context: you should NOT 'auf die Zähne beißen' when you're genuinely in pain — go to the doctor. The idiom is often used in reverse: 'don't grit your teeth, come to the doctor'.
To be on your guard — to watch out for something. A doctor may say 'Seien Sie auf der Hut bei [symptom]' = watch out if you notice [symptom]. Used for symptom monitoring.
To play it safe — better safe than sorry. A doctor often recommends 'auf Nummer sicher gehen' = run an extra test even if it's likely unnecessary. Worth following for visitors.
To get away with a black eye — to escape a bad situation with minor consequences. Fits a medical scare that ends OK — 'Glück gehabt: mit einem blauen Auge davongekommen'.
